question: In the 2016 study of multimorbidity in over 2,000 companion dogs attending private veterinary clinics in England, how did the number of diagnoses relate to age, and did body weight or breed have a significant effect on morbidity number?
answer: The number of diagnoses increased significantly with age; there was no significant effect of body weight or breed on morbidity number.

evidence.title: Multiple morbidities in companion dogs: a novel model for investigating age-related disease.
evidence.quote: In common with humans, we find that the number of diagnoses increases significantly with age in dogs. However, we find no significant weight or breed effects on morbidity number.

question: The 2016 English clinic study of multimorbidity in over 2,000 companion dogs found that breeds differ in longevity yet show similar age-related trajectories of morbidity number. What did the authors suggest is the likely source of the variation in lifespan across breeds?
answer: Differences in the age of onset of disease, rather than differences in the age-related trajectory of morbidity accumulation.

evidence.title: Multiple morbidities in companion dogs: a novel model for investigating age-related disease.
evidence.quote: This surprising result reveals that while breeds may vary in their average longevity and causes of death, their age-related trajectories of morbidities differ little, suggesting that age of onset of disease may be the source of variation in lifespan across breeds.

question: In the Dog Aging Project analysis of multimorbidity as a predictor of mortality, based on owner-reported data from over 50,000 dogs, which three conditions were highly prevalent across the multimorbidity combinations identified?

evidence.title: Multimorbidity as a predictor of mortality in companion dogs.
evidence.quote: Through classifying multimorbidities, we found that almost all either exhibit a synergistic effect or are driven by a single, predominant condition. In both cases, osteoarthritis, overweight, and cancer were highly prevalent throughout.

question: In the study comparing causes of death among over 40,000 sterilized and reproductively intact companion dogs, what association did sterilization have with lifespan, and which cause of death did it decrease and which did it increase?
answer: Sterilization was strongly associated with increased lifespan; it decreased the risk of death from infectious disease but increased the risk of death from cancer.

evidence.title: Reproductive capability is associated with lifespan and cause of death in companion dogs.
evidence.quote: We found that sterilization was strongly associated with an increase in lifespan, and while it decreased risk of death from some causes, such as infectious disease, it actually increased risk of death from others, such as cancer.

question: In the study of lifetime medical histories of 345 Rottweilers, what percentage of extreme-aged dogs (alive at the 95th percentile age at death, 13.3 years or older) died of cancer, compared with dogs of usual longevity (9-10 years)?
answer: 19% of extreme-aged dogs died of cancer versus 82% of dogs with usual longevity.

evidence.title: Exceptional longevity in pet dogs is accompanied by cancer resistance and delayed onset of major diseases.
evidence.quote: Extreme aged dogs (alive at the 95th percentile age at death for the study population, > or =13.3 years) were compared with a usual longevity group (9-10 years). Exceptional longevity in Rottweiler dogs was accompanied by a significant delay in the onset of major life-threatening diseases; 76% of extreme aged dogs remained free of all major diseases during the first 9 years of life. Only 19% of extreme aged dogs died of cancer versus 82% of dogs with usual longevity (p <.0001).

question: In the 2018 analysis of sex differences in aging that used two large independent databases of companion dog longevity and causes of death, how did the survival advantage by sex differ between intact and neutered dogs?
answer: Among intact dogs there was a small male survival advantage, whereas among neutered dogs there was a clear female survival advantage.

evidence.title: Do Female Dogs Age Differently Than Male Dogs?
evidence.quote: When broken down by neutering status, we discovered a small male advantage in survival among intact dogs but a clear female survival advantage among neutered dogs.

question: Before a veterinary clinical trial, 40 companion dogs with no history of cardiac pathology (at least 6 years old and at least 18 kg) were screened by Doppler echocardiography. How many were diagnosed with valvular regurgitation, how many of those were severe enough to be excluded from the trial, and in how many was a heart murmur detected by auscultation?
answer: 11 dogs had valvular regurgitation; 7 were severe enough to warrant exclusion; a heart murmur was detected by auscultation in only 1 case.

evidence.title: Asymptomatic heart valve dysfunction in healthy middle-aged companion dogs and its implications for cardiac aging.
evidence.quote: Eleven dogs from this cohort were diagnosed with valvular regurgitation by echocardiography, and seven of these cases were of sufficient severity to warrant exclusion from the clinical trial. In only one case was a heart murmur detected by auscultation.

question: In the echocardiographic screening study of 40 healthy middle-aged companion dogs (at least 6 years old, at least 18 kg) that revealed asymptomatic valvular regurgitation, which serum biochemistry analyte was significantly higher in dogs with moderate to severe valvular regurgitation than in the rest of the cohort?

evidence.title: Asymptomatic heart valve dysfunction in healthy middle-aged companion dogs and its implications for cardiac aging.
evidence.quote: Serum alkaline phosphatase levels were significantly higher in the dogs with moderate to severe valvular regurgitation compared to the rest of the cohort.

question: Among the 652 golden retrievers with known age that underwent necropsy at a veterinary academic center between 1989 and 2016, what proportion were determined to have died because of cancer, and how did the median age at death of dogs dying of cancer compare with those dying of other causes?
answer: 65.0% (424 of 652) died of cancer; median age at death was 9.83 years for cancer deaths versus 6.93 years for deaths from other causes.

evidence.title: Association of cancer-related mortality, age and gonadectomy in golden retriever dogs at a veterinary academic center (1989-2016).
evidence.quote: 424 of the 652 (65.0%) were determined to have died because of cancer. The median age for dying of a cause other than cancer was 6.93 years while those dying of cancer had a median age of 9.83 years (p<0.0001).

question: In the analysis of owner-reported lifespan and cause of death across 118 breeds (more than 40,000 dogs, restricted to completed birth cohorts to remove right-censoring bias), how did the percentage of old-age mortality and the proportional cancer mortality change with increasing breed body size?
answer: The percentage of old-age mortality decreased with increasing body size, while large size significantly increased proportional cancer mortality.

evidence.title: How size and genetic diversity shape lifespan across breeds of purebred dogs.
evidence.quote: Old age lifespan, as well as the percentage of old age mortality, decreased with increasing body size and increased with increasing genetic diversity. The lifespan of dogs dying of cancer followed the same patterns, but while large size significantly increased proportional cancer mortality, we could not detect a significant signal for lowered cancer mortality with increasing diversity.

question: In the Italian multi-centre study of 4957 dogs that died between 2004 and 2020 (records from 9 veterinary teaching hospitals and 2 public health institutions), what was the most frequent cause of death when classified by pathophysiologic process, and what was the most frequent when classified by organ system?
answer: By pathophysiologic process, neoplasia (34.0%), more frequent in large breeds; by organ system, diseases of the renal/urinary system (15.0%).

evidence.title: Factors related to longevity and mortality of dogs in Italy.
evidence.quote: The most frequent COD by PP was neoplasia (34.0%), which occurred more frequently in large breeds, namely German shepherd, Labrador retriever and Boxer. Degenerative diseases mostly affected small-sized dogs like Miniature pinscher and Dachshund. Regarding the OS involved, diseases of the renal/urinary system were most frequently responsible for COD (15.0%), prevalently degenerative and inflammatory/infectious.

question: In the VetCompass Australia study of Bullmastiff demography, longevity and mortality, what odds ratio was reported for the effect of neutering on death from urogenital disorders, and which specific diagnosis accounted for 41.7% of urogenital-related deaths?
answer: Neutering decreased the risk of urogenital death with an odds ratio of 0.14; pyometra accounted for 41.7% of urogenital-related deaths.

evidence.title: The Demography, Longevity and Mortality of Bullmastiffs Attending Veterinary Practices in Australia.
evidence.quote: The current study revealed that neutering decreased the risk (OR: 0.14) of death by a urogenital disorder, specifically pyometra which accounted for 41.7% of urogenital-related deaths.

question: Two owner-based mortality surveys of UK Kennel Club registered dogs reported leading causes of death: the breed-club questionnaire survey sent out in 2004 (15,881 deaths) and the survey of dogs registered with the Kennel Club in 2014 (5663 deceased dogs). What was the single most commonly reported cause of death in each survey, with its percentage?
answer: 2004 breed-club survey: cancer (27%), followed by old age (18%). 2014 Kennel Club survey: old age (13.8%), followed by unspecified cancer (8.7%).

evidence.title: Methods and mortality results of a health survey of purebred dogs in the UK.
evidence.quote: The most common causes of death were cancer (n=4282, 27%), "old age" (n=2830, 18%) and cardiac conditions (n=1770, 11%).

evidence.title: Longevity and mortality in Kennel Club registered dog breeds in the UK in 2014.
evidence.quote: The most commonly reported causes of death were old age (13.8%), unspecified cancer (8.7%) and heart failure (4.9%); with 5.1% of deaths reported as unknown cause.

notes: Synthesis across two surveys; the leading reported cause differs (cancer vs old age), partly reflecting how cancer was coded (unspecified vs any cancer).

question: In the survival analysis of 20,970 privately owned dogs from three independent primary care veterinary clinics in the United States, was gonadectomy associated with longer lifespan, in which sex was the effect stronger, and was the advantage retained in females that had already survived to ages 5 and 8 years?
answer: Yes, gonadectomy was associated with longer lifespan, more strongly in females than males, and the advantage was conserved in gonadectomized females that lived to at least 5 and 8 years.

evidence.title: Lifespan of companion dogs seen in three independent primary care veterinary clinics in the United States.
evidence.quote: Gonadectomy was associated with a longer lifespan, with the effect being stronger in females than in males. This lifespan advantage was conserved in gonadectomized female dogs that lived to at least ages 5 and 8 years.
